analytic.title: A Sufficient Condition for Rate Monotonic Schedulability Based on Response Time Analysis

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Rate Monotonic scheduling algorithm is widely used in real-time systems and embedded systems for its implementation simplicity and optimality in fixed priority scheduling. Since determining the schedulability of a task set in Rate Monotonic scheduling is an important step in designing a real-time system, schedulability analysis has been extensively studied. Although there is an exact schedulability test method for Rate Monotonic scheduling, the exact test is too complex to be executed on-line for large number of tasks because it is based on the response time calculation which is NP-hard. Thus many researchers studied on polynomial time sufficient conditions on Rate Monotonic schedulability. The existing polynomial time sufficient conditions are in the form of a utilization bound; that is, if a task set's total utilization is not larger than a utilization bound, the task set is accepted as schedulable one. Though the utilization bound tests are simple, they suffer from poor processor utilization. In this paper, we propose a new sufficient schedulability condition based on the response time test, different from the previous approaches. The new test provides a condition that is both necessary and sufficient for task sets with period ratio less than 2, while the previous tests provide only sufficient conditions. Extensive simulations show that our test significantly outperforms the existing tests with utilization bound.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Although the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) algorithm is optimal for preemptive [1] and non-preemptive [2] real-time scheduling on a uniprocessor, fixed priority scheduling such as the Rate Monotonic (RM) algorithm [1] has been more widely used in realtime systems because it is very easy to implement [3]. In [1], RM algorithm is proven to be optimal among all fixed priority scheduling schemes when tasks are scheduled independently and preemptively on a uniprocessor system. Liu and Layland also presented a sufficient condition for RM schedulability based on the concept of the "hard-to-schedule" task set. When there is a set of n periodic tasks, the task set is schedulable by the RM algorithm if the total utilization of the task set is less than or equal to n(2 1/n -1). Since the schedulability condition is on the processor utilization of a task set, the condition is often called "utilization bound."

After Liu and Layland's work, many researchers have studied on sufficient schedulability conditions to have schedulability bound tighter than Liu and Layland's bound. In [4], [5], they found a necessary and sufficient condition for RM schedulability. The condition is based on the concept of the worst case response time; that is, a task is schedulable if and only if the worst case response time of the task is shorter than its period (i.e., relative deadline). However, since the response time calculation is NP-hard [6], the exact analysis is not suited to be used for on-line admission control, especially when the number of tasks is large.

Other researchers studied to find a better (tighter) utilization bound than Liu and Layland's. In [3], [7], they proposed another form of utilization bound called the hyperbolic bound. It is proven in [3] the hyperbolic bound improves the acceptance ratio up to a limit of √ 2 for large n, compared with the Liu and Layland's. In [8], the utilization bound has been improved by considering additional information of a task set, period ratios. They proposed a schedulability condition that uses the maximum period ratio. The utilization bound using period ratios has been further generalized to utilization bound using the minimum and the maximum period ratios [9] and utilization bound using multiple period ratios [10].

In this paper, we propose a new sufficient condition for RM schedulability based on the response time analysis. Though the complexity of the proposed schedulability test is higher than existing utilization bound test, the proposed condition is a necessary and sufficient for task sets with the maximum period ratio less than 2. Extensive simulations show that our new test condition is significantly tighter than other utilization bound tests.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the task model and the assumptions made. Section 3 explains the previous schedulability tests based on utilization bounds in detail. Section 4 presents our new schedulability test based on the response time sufficient condition, and proves that the condition is in fact necessary and sufficient for task sets with the maximum period ratio less than 2. Section 5 compares the acceptance ratio of the proposed schedulability test and the existing ones. Finally, Section 6 concludes our work.

div.head: Definitions and assumptions
div.p: We first present some formal definitions before we discuss the schedulability. The task model is based on Liu and Layland's task model described in [1].

A periodic task is denoted as τ i . A periodic task set is represented by the collection of periodic tasks, τ = {τ i }. Each τ i is a two-tuple (T i , C i ) where T i is the period and C i is the worst case execution time. Note that T i ≥ C i > 0. This requires that if the first instance of τ i is invoked at time t x , the following instances are invoked periodically at t x + kT i , where k = 1, 2, 3, ..., and τ i must be allocated C i units of processor time in the interval
div.formula: [t x + (k -1)T i , t x + kT i ].
div.p: When an instance of τ i is invoked at time t and finishes at time t , tt is called "response time" of the instance. The worst case response time of τ i is defined as the maximum possible response time among all instances.

A concrete task has a specified release time, which is the time of the first activation. A concrete task set is schedulable if and only if the worst case response time of any concrete task τ i in the set is not larger than T i . A periodic task set is defined as schedulable if and only if all concrete task sets that are generated from the periodic task set are schedulable. In this paper, we consider only periodic task sets.
A summary of the assumptions used in this paper is given.
• Scheduling overhead can be ignored.

• There is no release jitter.(i.e., tasks become ready when arrive.) • Tasks are sorted in non-increasing order according to priority. For any pair of tasks τ i and τ j , if i < j, then, τ i has higher priority than τ j . • Tasks are all independent and cannot suspend themselves.

In RM scheduling, the shorter the period, the higher the priority. Thus in our paper, if i < j then T i < T j . The utilization factor of task τ i is given by U i = C i /T i which represents the fraction of processor time used by τ i in the worst case. The total utilization of a periodic task set τ is given by U τ = τ i ∈τ U i .

div.head: New schedulability test based on response time
div.p: The schedulability of a task in RM scheduling can be exactly determined by response time analysis [4], [5]. The worst case response time R i of a task τ i can be computed by:
div.formula: R i = C i + i-1 j=1 R i T j C j . (8
div.p: The worst case response time R i is the smallest value greater than zero satisfying the above equation. If R i ≤ T i for all τ i , the task set is schedulable by RM algorithm. Based on the response time analysis, we can obtain another sufficient condition for RM schedulability.

Proof:
div.formula: When C i + i-1 j=1 V i,k T j C j ≤ V i,k for some k, there must be a time t ≤ V i,k such that C i + i-1 j=1 t T j C j ≤ t which satisfies Equation (8). Thus, R i ≤ V i,k . From the definition of V i,k , we can see V i,k ≤ T i . Therefore, R i ≤ T i for all τ i .
div.p: We call the above condition as response time sufficient condition. The time complexity of the response time test given by Theorem 1 is O(n 3 ) in the worst case, higher than existing tests based on the hard-toschedule task set with O(n) (LL-test and hyperbolic bound) time complexity. However, the schedulability based on response time sufficient condition can accept more tasks than the other polynomial time tests. It is because, for task sets with maximum period ratio less than 2, the schedulability condition given in Theorem 1 is not only sufficient but also necessary for RM schedulability.

div.p: The above theorem tells us that any task set with total utilization lower than the hard-to-schedule task set must satisfy the response time sufficient condition. On the other hand, we can find a task set which has higher utilization than the hard-to-schedule task set, but satisfies the response time sufficient condition. However, the worst case response time of τ 5 is 55, and τ is schedulable by RM algorithm.

div.head: Simulation results
div.p: In this section, we compare the response time test with the existing utilization bound tests. The performance of a test is measured by acceptance ratio of each test normalized to that of the exact schedulability test. In our experiments, we have tested 5 task set groups, where each group has total utilization of 0.75, 0.80, 0.85, 0.90, and 0.95. Each task set group contains 40,000 task sets with period ratio greater than or equal to 2. Because the proposed schedulability condition is both necessary and sufficient for task sets with period ratio less than or equal to 2, we excluded task sets with period ratio less than 2 in our simulation. Task periods are randomly selected in [10, 1,000,000] with uniform distribution and utilization of a task is selected from 1% to 70% of the given total utilization also with uniform distribution.

Figure 1 shows the results of our simulation. The performance of the proposed test is very close to the exact test, though the performance slightly degrades with higher total utilization. To see the detailed behavior of the proposed test method, we also examine whether the number of tasks affects the performance. Figure 2 illustrates the performance of the schedulability tests when the number of tasks increases. As we can see from Figure 2, the performance of the proposed test method is little affected by the number of tasks, while the performance of the existing utilization bound tests degrades fast as the number of tasks increases.

Figure 3 shows the effect of the period ratios to the performance of the schedulability test methods. It turns out that when the period ratio is greater than 2, the performance of the tests is affected little by the period ratios. The performance of the existing schedulability tests depends on the total utilization and the number of task sets. With any period ratio, the proposed response time test outperforms the existing tests, and the performance is very close to the exact test, about 97% on the average.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we proposed a new polynomial time schedulability test method based on the response time analysis. The proposed test is a sufficient condition as the existing ones based on utilization bounds, but it is an exact test method for task sets with period ratio less than 2, while utilization bound tests are only sufficient conditions for the task sets. Extensive simulation shows that the performance of the proposed test method is very close to the exact schedulability analysis. The performance is almost 2 times better than the existing one using period ratios with low processor utilization, and 5 times with high processor utilization. This is due to the test policy that tries to check the last instances of the idle instant. The proposed schedulability test is shown to be optimal for task sets with period ratio less than 2. The behavior of the proposed method for task sets with higher period ratios needs further study. Also we plan to study the performance gap between the proposed method and the exact test.
